questions.answer: The two allotropes are diamond and graphite. In diamond, each carbon is bonded to four others, while in graphite, each is bonded to three others in planar layers.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell. Gaining four electrons to form a C4- anion would be difficult because the nucleus with six protons would struggle to hold on to ten total electrons (four extra electrons).

questions.answer: An oxygen atom has six electrons in its L shell and requires two more to complete its octet. Each oxygen atom shares two electrons with another oxygen atom. These two shared pairs of electrons constitute a double bond.

questions.raw_text: Describe the nature of covalent bonding in carbon, explaining why carbon forms this type of bond instead of ionic bonds, using methane as an example.

stem.text: Describe the nature of covalent bonding in carbon, explaining why carbon forms this type of bond instead of ionic bonds, using methane as an example.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell and needs to reach a noble gas configuration. It cannot form C4+ as it requires too much energy, nor C4- as the nucleus cannot hold 10 electrons. Thus, carbon shares its valence electrons. In methane (CH4), carbon shares its four valence electrons with four hydrogen atoms, each hydrogen contributing one electron to form four covalent bonds.

questions.raw_text: Discuss the physical properties of carbon compounds and explain how they relate to the nature of covalent bonding.

stem.text: Discuss the physical properties of carbon compounds and explain how they relate to the nature of covalent bonding.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: Most carbon compounds have low melting and boiling points because the intermolecular forces between their molecules are weak. These compounds are generally poor conductors of electricity because no charged ions are formed, as electrons are shared rather than transferred. The strong bonds exist within the molecule, but the weak forces between the molecules are why they have these properties.

questions.raw_text: Compare the structures of diamond and graphite, and explain how their different molecular arrangements result in different physical properties.

stem.text: Compare the structures of diamond and graphite, and explain how their different molecular arrangements result in different physical properties.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to four others to form a rigid 3D structure, making it the hardest substance. In graphite, each carbon atom is bonded to three others in a plane with a double bond, forming layers that can slide over one another, making it smooth and slippery. While their chemical properties are the same, their different structural arrangements lead to diamond's hardness and graphite's electrical conductivity and slipperiness.
